metadata.title: Chapter 2: Grammar: Verbs (क्रिया)
metadata.subject: Hindi
learning_outcomes: Understand the definition and importance of verbs (क्रिया) in Hindi grammar
Identify different types of verbs based on transitiveness (सकर्मक and अकर्मक)
Recognize how verbs change according to tense (काल), gender (लिंग), and number (वचन)
Correctly use root forms (धातु) and suffixes to construct meaningful Hindi sentences

ai_context.learning_goal: Students must comprehensively master the concept of verbs in Hindi, moving from basic action identification to advanced categorization based on objects and tenses.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the root form (धातु) with the complete infinitive verb (क्रिया).
Assuming every action verb must have a direct object in a sentence.
Forgetting to change the verb ending according to the gender and number of the subject or object.

blocks.title: The World Without Action
blocks.body: Imagine waking up in a universe where nothing moves. The sun hangs frozen in the sky, a bird is suspended mid-flight like a photograph, and you cannot speak, blink, or even think because all movement has stopped. Sounds terrifying, right? What makes our world vibrant and full of life is action! In grammar, these words of action hold the universe of a sentence together. Without them, nouns and pronouns are just statues standing in an empty room. Today, we step into the magical world of Hindi action words, known as verbs.

blocks.question: According to the hook story, what gives life and movement to a sentence in grammar?
options: Action words that bring movement and life
blocks.explanation: Action words (verbs) infuse life and movement into a sentence, just as action brings life to our physical world.

blocks.title: Concept 1: What is a Verb? (क्रिया का परिचय)
blocks.body: In Hindi grammar, a word that tells us about an action being done, an event taking place, or the state of a person or thing is called a [DICT_HINDI_KRIYA|क्रिया] (Verb). For example, in the sentence 'राम किताब पढ़ रहा है' (Ram is reading a book), the word 'पढ़ रहा है' is the verb because it tells us what Ram is doing. Verbs are the beating heart of any language. They tell us not only *what* is happening, but *when* it is happening (past, present, or future). Every complete sentence in Hindi requires a verb to make sense. If someone says 'बच्चa' (Child), you wait anxiously for the verb—is the child sleeping, crying, or playing? The suspense only ends when the verb arrives!

blocks.title: The 'Doing' Detective Game
blocks.body: Look around your room right now. Can you find five hidden actions? Spot a fan spinning (घूम रहा है), a clock ticking (चल रही है), dust settling (बैठ रही है), light shining (चमक रही है), and you breathing (सांस ले रहे हैं). You are surrounded by verbs every second of the day!

blocks.front: What is the primary function of a क्रिया (Verb) in a Hindi sentence?
blocks.back: To express an action, event, or state of being, bringing complete meaning to the sentence.

blocks.title: Concept 2: The Roots of Verbs – Dhatu (धातु)
blocks.body: Every big tree grows from a tiny seed. Similarly, every Hindi verb grows from a fundamental root called a [DICT_HINDI_DHATU|धातु] (Root). When you remove the '-na' ending from the infinitive form of a Hindi verb (like 'पढ़ना', 'लिखना', 'खाना'), what remains is the root. For example, the root of 'पढ़ना' (to read) is 'पढ़' (Padh). The root of 'लिखना' (to write) is 'लिख' (Likh). By adding various suffixes (प्रत्यय) like '-ना', '-ता', '-ते', '-ती', '-गा', '-गी', we transform these raw seeds into fully grown verbs that fit different tenses, subjects, and moods. Understanding the dhatu is the ultimate secret code to mastering Hindi verb conjugation!

blocks.question: If the infinitive verb is 'लिखना' (to write), what is its root (धातु)?
blocks.explanation: Removing the '-na' suffix from 'लिखना' leaves the raw root 'लिख' (Likh).

blocks.title: Concept 3: Transitive Verbs - Sakarmak Kriya (सकर्मक क्रिया)
blocks.body: Not all actions are created equal. Some actions reach out and grab an object, while others stay within the doer. When an action requires an object (कर्म) to complete its meaning, it is known as a [DICT_HINDI_SAKARMAK|सकर्मक क्रिया] (Transitive Verb). The word 'सकर्मक' literally means 'with an object' (स + कर्म). For instance, consider the sentence 'अमित सेब खा रहा है' (Amit is eating an apple). If you ask the question 'क्या खा रहा है?' (What is eating?), the answer is 'सेब' (apple). Because the action of eating directly affects the apple, 'खा रहा है' is a Sakarmak kriya. If you removed 'सेब' and just said 'अमित खा रहा है', the verb still demands to know *what* he is eating.

blocks.title: The 'Kya / Kisko' Test
blocks.body: To find out if a verb is Sakarmak (transitive), ask two golden questions before the verb: 'क्या' (What?) or 'किसको' (Whom?). If you get a logical answer from the sentence, the verb is transitive. Try it on 'माँ ने खाना पकाया'—Pakaaya (cooked) what? Khana (food). Transitive confirmed!

blocks.question: In the sentence 'रोहन ने पत्र लिखा' (Rohan wrote a letter), identify whether the verb is sakarmak and why.
options: Sakarmak, because the action passes onto the object 'पत्र' (letter)
blocks.explanation: Asking 'क्या लिखा?' yields 'पत्र', meaning the action has a direct object, making it Sakarmak.

blocks.title: Concept 4: Intransitive Verbs - Akarmak Kriya (अकर्मक क्रिया)
blocks.body: On the other side of the spectrum, we have [DICT_HINDI_AKARMAK|अकर्मक क्रिया] (Intransitive Verbs). The word 'अकर्मक' means 'without an object' (अ + कर्म). In these verbs, the action's effect stays entirely with the subject (कर्ता). There is no object involved! For example, consider 'पक्षी आकाश में उड़ रहे हैं' (Birds are flying in the sky). If you ask 'क्या उड़ रहे हैं?' (What are flying?), the sky is not what is being flown—the birds themselves are doing the flying. There is no direct object. Other classic examples include सोना (to sleep), हँसना (to laugh), रोना (to cry), and दौड़ना (to run). You cannot 'sleep an apple' or 'laugh a chair'! These verbs are complete all by themselves.

blocks.front: What is the key difference between Sakarmak and Akarmak verbs?
blocks.back: Sakarmak verbs require a direct object to complete their action, whereas Akarmak verbs do not need an object and the action remains with the subject.

blocks.question: Which of the following sentences contains an Akarmak (intransitive) verb?
options: बालक दूध पी रहा है (The boy is drinking milk)
सोहन मैदान में दौड़ रहा है (Sohan is running in the field)
अध्यापक पाठ पढ़ा रहे हैं (The teacher is teaching the lesson)
blocks.explanation: Running (दौड़ रहा है) is an action contained within the subject. 'मैदान में' is a location, not a direct object.

blocks.title: Concept 5: Verbs and Tense (काल का प्रभाव)
blocks.body: Verbs are shape-shifters. They change their appearance based on when the action happens. This is called Tense ([DICT_HINDI_KRIYA|काल]). Hindi has three main tenses: Past (भूतकाल), Present (वर्तमान काल), and Future (भविष्यत् काल). When Rahul ate yesterday, the verb was 'खाया' (Past). When Rahul eats right now, it is 'खा रहा है' (Present). When Rahul will eat tomorrow, it becomes 'खाएगा' (Future). Notice how the root 'खा' (Khaa) remains the constant foundation, while the endings morph dynamically to anchor the sentence in time. Mastering verb tenses allows you to tell stories spanning across centuries or predict tomorrow's adventures!

blocks.title: Time Travel with Verbs
blocks.body: Take a simple verb root like 'चल' (Walk). Say it in three time dimensions aloud: Yesterday ('चला'), Today ('चल रहा है'), Tomorrow ('चल एगा'). Notice how your mouth shapes different endings while the core root stays identical!

blocks.front: What are the three main categories of Kaal (Tense) that affect Hindi verbs?
blocks.back: 1. भूतकाल (Past Tense), 2. वर्तमान काल (Present Tense), 3. भविष्यत् काल (Future Tense).

blocks.title: Concept 6: Gender and Number Agreement (लिंग और वचन)
blocks.body: Unlike English, where verbs remain largely neutral regardless of who is performing them (e.g., 'The boy runs' and 'The girl runs'), Hindi verbs are extremely polite and adapt to the gender ([DICT_HINDI_KRIYA|लिंग]) and number ([DICT_HINDI_KRIYA|वचन]) of the subject or object. If a boy is going, we say 'लड़का जाता है'. If a girl is going, the verb magically transforms into 'लड़की जाती है'! If multiple boys are going, it becomes 'लड़के जाते हैं'. This agreement ensures that the sentence flows in harmonious balance. The verb mirrors the characteristics of the noun it serves.

blocks.question: Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: 'घोड़ा तेज़ ___ रहा है।' (The horse is running fast.)
blocks.explanation: Wait, let's look at standard options: [दौड़ रही है, दौड़ रहा है, दौड़ रहे हैं]. Correct is 'दौड़ रहा है' because 'घोड़ा' is singular masculine.

blocks.title: Summary of Verb Architecture
blocks.body: Let's review our master blueprint for Hindi verbs. We started with verbs ([DICT_HINDI_KRIYA|क्रिया]) as life-giving action words. We dug deeper to find their raw seeds, the [DICT_HINDI_DHATU|धातु]. We split actions into those that require objects ([DICT_HINDI_SAKARMAK|सकर्मक]) and those that are self-contained ([DICT_HINDI_AKARMAK|अकर्मक]). Finally, we saw how verbs dance to the tune of time (काल), gender (लिंग), and number (वचन). With these rules in your toolkit, you are fully equipped to construct any sentence with absolute grammatical precision.

blocks.question: Which term describes the raw, uninflected core of a Hindi verb from which all forms are derived?
blocks.explanation: The धातु is the foundational root from which all conjugated verb forms sprout.
